scope: Past Written Papers (PP) series retrieval index. One entry per paper and one per question. This file is an INDEX, not a content source: answer text lives only in the paper spec. Regenerate with build_index.py; never hand-edit.
naming_convention: QP<YY><MM>.html, where QP = Question Paper, YY = year and MM = month of the sitting (QP2607 = July 2026); question_id QP<YY><MM>-Q<n>; anchors #q1..#q9
source_of_truth_policy: specs/<PAPER>.json is authoritative for content. This manifest is authoritative for retrieval. Both index pages and the paper page are generated; editing generated HTML is always wrong.

recurrence_statuses.single: Set once in the sittings MIW has transcribed. NOT "never asked before".
recurrence_statuses.first: Earliest sitting of a family that returns at a later sitting.
recurrence_statuses.repeat_exact: Later sitting; normalised printed stem identical to the first.
recurrence_statuses.repeat_near: Later sitting; printed stem materially reworded.

recurrence_rule: Canonical recurrence is computed chronologically in recurrence_model.py from (year, month) over MIW's own transcriptions, and from nothing else. The source copy host's printed annotation is discovery-only provenance held in the spec as host_recurrence_hint and is never published; the authoring field recurrence_class records production order, not sitting order. Every count here is scoped to the sittings MIW has transcribed.

paper_status_model.available: Answers are published for this sitting.
paper_status_model.coming_later: No answers yet. Covers every case a student cannot act on -- not transcribed, in production, or source copy held only. Holding a source copy never reads as solved.

questions.question_text: Improvements in Rudder efficiency can considerably contribute to improving propulsion effectiveness. Discuss common rudder-efficiency improvements devices/ techniques currently in use, referring to the following: (a) Rudder Thrust Fins (b) Asymmetric Rudders (c) Rudder Bulbs (d) Grim Vane Wheels
questions.short_title: Rudder Efficiency Improvement Devices
regulations: MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 as revised by MEPC.328(76) - the Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index and the operational Carbon Intensity Indicator, applicable from 1 January 2023 (context and driver only; no value or boundary asserted)
Initial IMO Strategy on reduction of GHG emissions from ships, 2018 - the operative IMO strategy at this sitting
ISO 19030 - measurement of changes in hull and propeller performance (industry standard)
questions.family_summary: First set here. The same task returns at April 2024 Q4, September 2024 Q9, June 2025 Q1.
questions.verification_status: Device physics and the four named devices carried across from the MIW verification record for QP2404 Q4, where the hydrodynamic mechanisms were established; nothing in that material is date-dependent. The regulatory framing was re-derived from first principles for a January 2023 sitting rather than inherited: MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 as revised by MEPC.328(76), with the EEXI and CII requirements applying from 1 January 2023, and the Initial IMO GHG Strategy of 2018 as the operative strategy. Percentage gains are stated as manufacturers' claims at design condition, never as verified savings.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the EEXI and operational CII requirements became applicable on 1 January 2023
reverify_before_publication.why: Correct, and central to dating this answer. It is stated as newly applicable at the sitting. Before publication confirm the wording still reads as a sitting-date statement and has not drifted into the present tense of a later regime.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The percentage gain ranges quoted for each of the four devices
reverify_before_publication.why: Manufacturer and model-test claims at design condition, taken from industry literature rather than from verified full-scale trials. Published ranges differ widely. Stated as claims; nothing in the answer depends on a particular figure.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That Grim vane wheels largely fell out of service through blade fatigue and loss
reverify_before_publication.why: Established from industry and technical-press accounts, not from a manufacturer's or class failure report read this session.

Who is responsible for payment of award to the salvor, for salvage of maritime property, as per the salvage convention? Which form popularly used in case of contractual salvage? How is the amount of award calculated .JS per this form?
questions.short_title: Maritime Against Contractual Salvage, Liability for the Award, and Lloyd's Open Form
regulations: International Convention on Salvage, 1989 - adopted 28 April 1989, IN FORCE 14 JULY 1996. Twenty-seven years old at this sitting and unmoved between this paper and its donor.
Salvage Convention 1989 - the definition of a salvage operation, and the three preconditions derived from it: a recognised subject in danger, a voluntary service, and success.

Salvage Convention 1989 Article 8 - the duties of the salvor to carry out the operations with due care, to exercise due care to prevent or minimise damage to the environment, to seek assistance from other salvors where reasonably required, and to accept the intervention of other salvors when reasonably requested; and the corresponding duties of the owner and master to co-operate, to exercise due care to prevent or minimise environmental damage, and to accept redelivery when the property is brought to a place of safety.

Salvage Convention 1989 Article 13 - the criteria for fixing the reward, and the rule that the reward is paid by all of the vessel and other property interests IN PROPORTION TO THEIR RESPECTIVE SALVED VALUES. The reward, exclusive of interest and costs, may not exceed the salved value of the vessel and other property.

Salvage Convention 1989 Article 14 - special compensation where the salvor has carried out operations in respect of a vessel which by herself or her cargo threatened damage to the environment, PAYABLE BY THE SHIPOWNER, with an increase where environmental damage was actually prevented or minimised.

Salvage Convention 1989 - the annulment and modification of contracts entered into under undue influence or the influence of danger where the terms are inequitable, or where the payment is excessive or grossly inadequate.

Lloyd's Standard Form of Salvage Agreement (Lloyd's Open Form) - LOF 2020 is the edition current at this sitting. Described by substance; NO CLAUSE IS QUOTED OR CITED BY NUMBER because no form is held.
SCOPIC - the Special Compensation P&I Clause, a contractual alternative to Article 14 incorporated into LOF by agreement. Described by substance; no tariff rate is asserted.

Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 - the Indian statute in force at this sitting, giving effect to the salvage regime in Indian law. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026 and is THIRTY-SEVEN MONTHS FUTURE.

questions.short_title: Effective Communication under the ISM Code, Engine Resource Management, and Communication Failure
regulations: International Safety Management (ISM) Code, as amended through MSC.353(92) - the edition operative at this sitting.

ISM Code - the requirement that the Company establishes and uses a working language, that the safety management system documentation is in a language understood by personnel, and that translation is provided where it is not.

ISM Code - the requirement that personnel are able to communicate effectively in the execution of their duties related to the safety management system. This is the provision closest to the phrase the stem uses.
ISM Code - familiarisation of new personnel and personnel transferred to new assignments, and the identification and documentation of essential instructions before sailing.
ISM Code - reporting of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences to the Company, with investigation, analysis and corrective action.

ISM Code - the master's responsibility and authority, including the duty to issue appropriate orders and instructions IN A CLEAR AND SIMPLE MANNER, to verify that specified requirements are observed, and to review the safety management system and report its deficiencies to shore-based management.
ISM Code - the designation of a person or persons ashore having DIRECT ACCESS TO THE HIGHEST LEVEL OF MANAGEMENT, providing a link between the Company and those on board.
ISM Code - document control, including the prompt removal of obsolete documents.
ISM Code - emergency preparedness, the response organisation, and drills and exercises.
ISM Code - internal safety audits, the review of the safety management system, and the Company's evaluation of its effectiveness.
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 - the Indian statute in force at this sitting giving effect to the ISM Code. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026 and is thirty-seven months future.

regulations: Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 (Act 9 of 1856) - IN FORCE at this sitting. Its first section vests in the consignee named in the bill of lading, and in the endorsee to whom property in the goods passes upon or by reason of the consignment or endorsement, all rights of suit and the same liabilities in respect of the goods as if the contract contained in the bill of lading had been made with himself; the shipper's own liability for freight is preserved. REPEALED by the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 with effect from 10 September 2025 - thirty-one months AFTER this sitting.

Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925, as amended by the amending Act of 1993 - IN FORCE at this sitting. It is the vehicle by which the HAGUE-VISBY RULES have effect in Indian law, its Schedule setting out the Rules. REPEALED and re-enacted with modifications by the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 with effect from 10 September 2025 - thirty-one months AFTER this sitting.

The Hague-Visby Rules as scheduled to the 1925 Act - the carrier's obligation to exercise DUE DILIGENCE BEFORE AND AT THE BEGINNING OF THE VOYAGE to make the ship seaworthy, properly man, equip and supply her, and make the cargo spaces fit and safe; the obligation to load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods properly and carefully; the shipper's right to demand a bill showing the leading marks, the number of packages or pieces or the quantity or weight, and the apparent order and condition of the goods, subject to the proviso that the carrier need not state what he has no reasonable means of checking; the escalation of that description from prima facie evidence to conclusive evidence once the bill has been transferred to a third party acting in good faith; the one-year time bar; the package or unit and weight limitation, whose unit of account is the Special Drawing Right; and the nullity of any clause relieving or lessening the carrier's liability otherwise than as the Rules provide. NO ARTICLE OR RULE IS ASSERTED BY NUMBER ANYWHERE IN THIS ANSWER - see unresolved.
Indian Sale of Goods Act, 1930 - includes the bill of lading within the definition of a document of title to goods, which is the statutory anchor in Indian law for the document-of-title function.
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 - the governing Indian shipping statute at this sitting. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026 and is THIRTY-SEVEN MONTHS FUTURE.
Hamburg Rules (United Nations Convention on the Carriage of Goods by Sea, 1978) - INDIA IS NOT A PARTY. Not applicable to any Indian bill at this sitting.
Rotterdam Rules (United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Carriage of Goods Wholly or Partly by Sea, 2008) - NOT IN FORCE at this sitting.

MARPOL Annex VI regulations 23 and 25 - the attained EEXI for existing ships and the required EEXI reduction factor. APPLICABLE FROM 1 JANUARY 2023, six weeks before this sitting. A high-efficiency propeller is one of the design measures by which the attained value is reduced. The reduction-factor framework itself is treated at Q3 of this paper and is not restated here.

MARPOL Annex VI regulation 28 - the annual operational carbon intensity indicator and the A to E rating. APPLICABLE FROM 1 JANUARY 2023. AT THIS SITTING NO SHIP HELD A RATING: the first rating year began six weeks earlier and the rating is determined only after the calendar year ends. A propeller improvement lowers fuel per tonne-mile and therefore improves the rating, which is why it is one of the few measures that serve both the design index and the operational rating.

MARPOL Annex VI - the enhanced SEEMP including the Part III carbon intensity plan, required on board from 1 January 2023, under the 2022 Guidelines adopted by resolution MEPC.346(78). The vehicle in which a planned propeller retrofit and its expected effect are recorded.
Initial IMO Strategy on reduction of GHG emissions from ships, resolution MEPC.304(72) of 2018 - THE OPERATIVE STRATEGY AT THIS SITTING, and recited in the preamble of MEPC.328(76) itself.

questions.short_title: MLC 2006 - Flag and Port State Responsibilities, Complaint Procedures, Detainable Deficiencies, and Indian Grievance Redressal
regulations: Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 (ILO) - IN FORCE 20 AUGUST 2013. AT THIS SITTING THE OPERATIVE TEXT IS THE CONVENTION AS AMENDED THROUGH THE 2018 AMENDMENTS. The 2014 amendments (abandonment and financial security), the 2016 amendments (harassment and bullying, effective 8 January 2019) and the 2018 amendments (wages while held captive, effective 26 December 2020) are all in force.

MLC 2006 Article VI - the Regulations and Part A of the Code are mandatory, Part B contains Guidelines; substantial equivalence is permitted for Part A, BUT NOT for Part A of the Code within Title 5, whose compliance machinery must be implemented as written.

MLC 2006 Article V paragraph 4 - the basis on which a foreign ship may be inspected in the port of any Member. Article V paragraph 7 - NO MORE FAVOURABLE TREATMENT for ships of States that have not ratified.

MLC 2006 Article XIII establishes the ILO SPECIAL TRIPARTITE COMMITTEE, whose mandate is to keep the working of the Convention under continuous review. ARTICLE XV is the procedure by which the CODE is amended, on the Committee's recommendation - NOT by IMO tacit acceptance. A ratifying Member is not bound by an amendment if it expresses formal disagreement within the prescribed period.
MLC 2006 Regulation 5.1.1 and Standard A5.1.1 - flag State general principles; the effective system of inspection and certification; a copy of the Convention on board.
MLC 2006 Regulation 5.1.2 and Standard A5.1.2 - authorization of recognized organizations, with the flag State remaining FULLY RESPONSIBLE and the current list provided to the ILO and made public.

MLC 2006 Regulation 5.1.3 and Standard A5.1.3 - the Maritime Labour Certificate and the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance. Ships of 500 gross tonnage and over on international voyages or operating from or between foreign ports; others on request. Five years' validity with an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary dates; interim certificate six months. DMLC PART I BY THE COMPETENT AUTHORITY, PART II BY THE SHIPOWNER.

MLC 2006 Regulation 5.1.4 and Standard A5.1.4 - inspection and enforcement. The interval between inspections SHALL IN NO CASE EXCEED THREE YEARS. Qualified, independent inspectors with power to board, examine, require rectification and PROHIBIT THE SHIP FROM SAILING; rights of appeal; confidentiality of the source of any complaint; no conflict of interest; reports to the authority and the master and posted on board; an annual report; adequate penalties.

MLC 2006 Regulation 5.1.5 and Standard A5.1.5 - ON-BOARD COMPLAINT PROCEDURES. Fair, effective and expeditious handling; resolution at the lowest level as the design preference, WITHOUT prejudice to the right to complain directly to the master or to external authorities; a copy of the procedures to every seafarer with contact information and the name of an impartial adviser on board; the right to be accompanied or represented; and the PROHIBITION AND PENALIZATION OF VICTIMIZATION for filing a complaint.
MLC 2006 Regulation 5.1.6 - an official inquiry into any serious marine casualty causing injury or loss of life.

MLC 2006 Regulation 5.2.1 and Standard A5.2.1 - inspections in port. The certificate and DMLC ACCEPTED AS PRIMA FACIE EVIDENCE; inspection limited to the Articles, the Regulations and Part A only of the Code; FOUR TRIGGERS for a more detailed inspection; and TWO GROUNDS FOR DETENTION - conditions clearly hazardous to the safety, health or security of seafarers, or a serious or repeated breach of the requirements including seafarers' rights. Rectification or an accepted plan of action; the flag State notified forthwith; COMPENSATION FOR UNDUE DETENTION OR DELAY.

MLC 2006 Regulation 5.2.2 and Standard A5.2.2 - ONSHORE SEAFARER COMPLAINT-HANDLING PROCEDURES. Complaint to an authorized officer in port; initial investigation; resolution sought at ship level; notification to the flag State for advice and a corrective plan of action; escalation to the Director-General of the ILO; confidentiality of the source safeguarded.

MLC 2006 Regulation 5.3 and Standard A5.3 - LABOUR-SUPPLYING RESPONSIBILITIES, with Regulation 1.4 and Standard A1.4 on recruitment and placement services: licensing and regulation, registers, verification of employment agreements, the PROHIBITION ON CHARGING FEES TO THE SEAFARER save for the statutory medical, seafarer's book and passport, and a SYSTEM OF PROTECTION to compensate the seafarer for monetary loss arising from the service's failure.

MLC 2006 Regulation 2.5 and Standard A2.5.2 - abandonment and financial security, introduced by the 2014 amendments and IN FORCE at this sitting: a certificate posted on board, direct access by the seafarer, and cover for outstanding wages, repatriation and essential needs.

ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE: the amendments approved by the International Labour Conference at its 110th Session in 2022 - IN FORCE 23 DECEMBER 2024, TWENTY-TWO MONTHS AFTER THIS SITTING. Nothing from that set is presented as an obligation.
PROHIBITED AS FUTURE: the amendments approved by the 113th International Labour Conference in June 2025 - twenty-eight months after this sitting. Never cited.

Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (India) - THE DOMESTIC STATUTE IN FORCE AT THIS SITTING, and the vehicle for India's flag State, port State and labour-supplying obligations. The maritime administration is the DIRECTORATE GENERAL OF SHIPPING. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026 - THIRTY-SEVEN MONTHS FUTURE - and the administration was renamed at that point; neither appears in this answer. NO SECTION OF THE 1958 ACT IS CITED BY NUMBER.

questions.question_text: Compare and discuss the basic features of CLC’92 and Bunker Convention2001, with specific reference to the type of ships, 0il & nature of pollution damages covered, limits of liability and geographical coverage.
questions.short_title: CLC 1992 Against the Bunker Convention 2001 - Ships, Oil and Damage, Limits of Liability, and Geographical Coverage
regulations: International Convention on Civil Liability for Oil Pollution Damage, 1992 (CLC'92) - IN FORCE 30 MAY 1996, twenty-seven years before this sitting. Applies to any sea-going vessel or seaborne craft of any type whatsoever CONSTRUCTED OR ADAPTED FOR THE CARRIAGE OF PERSISTENT HYDROCARBON MINERAL OIL IN BULK AS CARGO. The 1992 Protocol DELIBERATELY EXTENDED the Convention to LADEN AND UNLADEN TANKERS ALIKE, INCLUDING SPILLS OF THEIR OWN BUNKER OIL - one of the principal changes from CLC 1969, which reached only ships actually carrying oil in bulk as cargo. The 'ACTUALLY CARRYING' PROVISO IS CONFINED TO A COMBINATION CARRIER - a ship capable of carrying oil AND other cargoes - which is a ship under the Convention only while actually carrying oil in bulk as cargo and on any voyage following unless it is proved that no residues remain.

CLC'92 - the definition of pollution damage: loss or damage caused outside the ship by contamination resulting from the escape or discharge of oil, with compensation for impairment of the environment other than loss of profit LIMITED TO THE COSTS OF REASONABLE MEASURES OF REINSTATEMENT ACTUALLY UNDERTAKEN OR TO BE UNDERTAKEN; and the costs of preventive measures and further loss or damage caused by preventive measures.

CLC'92 - STRICT LIABILITY of the registered owner, subject to three defences: act of war, hostilities, civil war or insurrection, or an exceptional, inevitable and irresistible natural phenomenon; damage wholly caused by the act or omission of a third party done with intent to cause damage; and damage wholly caused by the negligence of a government or other authority responsible for maintaining lights or other navigational aids. Contributory fault of the claimant reduces or exonerates liability.

CLC'92 - CHANNELLING. Liability rests on the registered owner ALONE, and no claim for pollution damage may be made against the servants or agents of the owner or members of the crew, the pilot, the charterer, the manager or operator, the salvor, or persons taking preventive measures, unless the damage resulted from their personal act or omission committed with intent or recklessly and with knowledge that such damage would probably result.

CLC'92 - LIMITATION. The Convention contains ITS OWN limitation regime, banded by the ship's tonnage with an overall ceiling, the fund being constituted with the court or other competent authority of a State Party and distributed among pollution claimants. The right to limit is lost where the damage resulted from the owner's personal act or omission committed with intent, or recklessly and with knowledge that such damage would probably result. NO FIGURE IS ASSERTED - see unresolved.

CLC'92 - COMPULSORY INSURANCE. Required of the registered owner of a ship carrying MORE THAN 2,000 TONS OF PERSISTENT OIL IN BULK AS CARGO, evidenced by a certificate carried on board, with a right of DIRECT ACTION against the insurer, who may invoke the defences available to the owner and may limit even where the owner has lost that right.

1992 Fund Convention and the 2003 Supplementary Fund Protocol - the SECOND AND THIRD TIERS behind CLC, financed by contributions from receivers of contributing oil cargo. Named as the structure that has no counterpart under the Bunker Convention. NO FUND LIMIT OR CEILING IS ASSERTED.

International Convention on Civil Liability for Bunker Oil Pollution Damage, 2001 - ADOPTED 23 MARCH 2001, IN FORCE 21 NOVEMBER 2008, fourteen years before this sitting. Applies to ANY SEAGOING VESSEL AND SEABORNE CRAFT OF ANY TYPE WHATSOEVER.

Bunker Convention 2001 - 'BUNKER OIL' means any hydrocarbon mineral oil, INCLUDING LUBRICATING OIL, used or intended to be used for the operation or propulsion of the ship, and any residues of such oil. PERSISTENCE IS NOT REQUIRED.

Bunker Convention 2001 - 'SHIPOWNER' includes the registered owner, the bareboat charterer, the manager and the operator, who are JOINTLY AND SEVERALLY LIABLE. Liability is strict, subject to the same three defences as CLC.

Bunker Convention 2001 - EXCLUSION OF CLC DAMAGE. The Convention does not apply to pollution damage as defined in CLC, WHETHER OR NOT COMPENSATION IS PAYABLE IN RESPECT OF IT UNDER THAT CONVENTION. Warships and State ships on non-commercial service are also excluded.

Bunker Convention 2001 - LIMITATION. The Convention SETS NO LIMIT OF ITS OWN. It preserves the shipowner's right to limit under any applicable national or international regime, in practice the Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims as amended, so a bunker pollution claim competes within the GENERAL limitation fund for the incident. THERE IS NO SECOND-TIER FUND. NO LLMC FIGURE AND NO LLMC RESOLUTION NUMBER IS ASSERTED - see unresolved.

Bunker Convention 2001 - COMPULSORY INSURANCE. Required of the REGISTERED OWNER of a ship of MORE THAN 1,000 GROSS TONNAGE registered in a State Party, up to the applicable limit, evidenced by a certificate in the annexed model form carried on board, with DIRECT ACTION against the insurer; and States Parties enforce the certificate requirement against ships of ANY FLAG entering their ports or offshore facilities.

GEOGRAPHICAL APPLICATION - IDENTICAL IN BOTH. Pollution damage caused in the territory, including the territorial sea, of a State Party; pollution damage caused in the exclusive economic zone of a State Party or, where none has been established, in an equivalent area beyond and adjacent to the territorial sea determined in accordance with international law and extending not more than 200 NAUTICAL MILES from the baselines; and PREVENTIVE MEASURES, WHEREVER TAKEN, to prevent or minimise such damage.

HNS Convention - named in one sentence only, as the third element completing the liability map alongside CLC and the Bunker Convention. NO CLAIM ABOUT ITS STATUS, RATIFICATION OR ENTRY INTO FORCE IS MADE ANYWHERE IN THIS ANSWER.

questions.verification_status: VERIFIED FOR PILOT REVIEW. The printed stem was transcribed from the born-digital text layer without retyping and reconciled character by character against both pages rendered at 200 dpi; the two printed anomalies in this stem - '0il' with a ZERO for 'Oil', and 'Convention2001' with the space missing - are preserved in text_verbatim and are recorded in the paper anchor at section 1.4. THE STRUCTURAL FINDING OF THIS VERIFICATION IS THAT THE STEM PRINTS NO LIMBS BUT NAMES FOUR REQUIRED HEADS IN CONTINUOUS PROSE - the type of ships, the oil and nature of the pollution damage covered, the limits of liability, and the geographical coverage - and the answer is built as four heads in the printed order because there is no lettering to count against and the fourth is habitually dropped. THE DONOR IS THE CLOSEST IN THE ENTIRE BATCH AND IT IS THE REASON THIS BRANCH'S BASELINE WAS REFRESHED. QP2304-Q7 sits at April 2023, TWO MONTHS after this sitting; before its integration the nearest donor was twelve or nineteen months away. The relation is NEAR WITH REVERSED FRAMING: the donor asks the candidate to describe the Bunker Convention and say how it differs from CLC, across four limbs of which ONLY ONE - liability and limitation - corresponds to a head printed here. The donor's TIME LIMITS limb is deliberately NOT carried, because this paper does not print that head; importing good donor material that answers a different question is the specific failure mode a two-month donor invites, and it is recorded as a scope decision rather than a temporal one. Two of this paper's heads - the type of ships, and the geographical coverage - are not limbs of the donor at all and are authored fresh. TEMPORAL RISK IS LOW AND STRUCTURALLY SO. CLC 1992 entered into force on 30 May 1996 and the Bunker Convention, adopted 23 March 2001, on 21 November 2008 - twenty-seven and fourteen years before this sitting. No amendment, protocol or entry into force touching either instrument falls in the two-month donor window. The donor was nevertheless audited line by line rather than assumed clean, precisely because two months is the distance at which an audit gets skipped, and the further siblings QP2409-Q6 and QP2402-Q2 were read as cross-checks and contributed nothing. THE ONE ITEM THE AUDIT FOUND IS EVIDENTIAL AND NOT TEMPORAL, AND THE DISTINCTION IS RECORDED SO THAT A LATER READER DOES NOT MISTAKE IT. The donor states the CLC limitation figures; they derive from the 2000 amendments, in force since 2003, and are temporally safe. THEY ARE NOT ASSERTED HERE. Under anchor section 5.2 item 1 NO SDR FIGURE, NO TONNAGE BAND, NO LIMITATION AMOUNT, NO FUND CEILING AND NO CURRENCY CONVERSION APPEARS ANYWHERE IN THIS ANSWER, even though the printed stem names 'limits of liability' as a required head. That head is answered to the STRUCTURE of limitation - CLC carrying its own tonnage-banded limit, a dedicated fund constituted with the court and reserved to pollution claimants, and two cargo-financed tiers behind it, against the Bunker Convention setting no limit of its own, referring out to the applicable regime so that the claim shares one general fund with every other claim from the incident, and having no second tier at all - which is what a comparison requires in any event and is more discriminating than a pair of numbers. The answer says positively that no figure is given and why, so that a candidate does not supply one. THE EVIDENCE LEVEL IS STATED HONESTLY AND IS LOW. questions.question_text: A. One of the objectives of UNCLOS is protection of marine environment and prevention of pollution. Define pollution as per UNCLOS and discuss the key features of obligations of coastal states in this regard. B. State the 3 main tiers of the oil pollution damage compensation conventions of the IMO. In each case elaborate one who is responsible for payment of compensation. Also, state the source of funds as well as certification required by ship under each tier.
questions.short_title: UNCLOS Pollution Definition, Coastal State Obligations, and the Three Compensation Tiers
regulations: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, 1982, in force 16 November 1994 - UNAMENDED, so the held text is the text at this sitting
UNCLOS article 1(1)(4) - the definition of pollution of the marine environment. Read verbatim at source in this session
UNCLOS article 192 - the general obligation of States to protect and preserve the marine environment
UNCLOS article 193 - the sovereign right to exploit natural resources, exercised in accordance with the duty to protect and preserve

UNCLOS article 194 - measures to prevent, reduce and control pollution from any source, by the best practicable means and in accordance with capabilities, and article 194(2) on damage to other States; and article 195, a separate article, carrying the duty not to transfer damage or hazards from one area to another or transform one type of pollution into another
UNCLOS articles 207, 210, 211 and 212 - rule-making for land-based sources, dumping, pollution from vessels, and pollution from or through the atmosphere
UNCLOS articles 217, 218 and 220 - enforcement by flag States, port States and coastal States
UNCLOS article 221 - measures to avoid pollution arising from maritime casualties
UNCLOS article 235 - responsibility and liability, including the obligation to ensure recourse for prompt and adequate compensation. Read verbatim at source
International Convention on Civil Liability for Oil Pollution Damage, 1992 - tier one. NO TEXT HELD by MIW; cited by identity, no article asserted and NO MONETARY LIMIT STATED

International Convention on the Establishment of an International Fund for Compensation for Oil Pollution Damage, 1992 - tier two. NO TEXT HELD; cited by identity, no article asserted and NO MONETARY LIMIT STATED
Protocol of 2003 establishing the Supplementary Fund - tier three. NO TEXT HELD; cited by identity, no article asserted and NO MONETARY LIMIT STATED
Bunkers Convention 2001 and the HNS Convention - named only to be excluded from the three tiers. Not held and not quoted

Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (India), administered by DG Shipping - the statute giving effect to these conventions in Indian law at this sitting. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 is three years future and is not cited

THIS IS THE ONLY QUESTION ON THE PAPER WHERE THE HELD TEXT IS THE SITTING TEXT. UNCLOS entered into force on 16 November 1994 and is UNAMENDED, so the corpus copy is the text a March 2023 candidate was examined on, and there is no reversal of any kind to perform on limb A. THE DEFINITION WAS READ VERBATIM AT SOURCE. Article 1, paragraph 1, sub-paragraph (4) of the Convention defines pollution of the marine environment as the introduction by man, directly or indirectly, of substances or energy into the marine environment, including estuaries, which results or is likely to result in such deleterious effects as harm to living resources and marine life, hazards to human health, hindrance to marine activities including fishing and other legitimate uses of the sea, impairment of quality for use of sea water, and reduction of amenities. ARTICLES 192, 193, 194 AND 235 WERE ALSO READ VERBATIM at source in this session and are quoted or paraphrased only from that reading. The remaining Part XII articles - 207, 210, 211, 212, 217, 218, 220, 221 - are cited by identity and their substance is carried from MIW's own verification record for QP2309-Q8, where it was established against the same held text. THE PART XII SAFEGUARDS IN SECTION 7 ARE REFERRED TO IN GENERAL TERMS ONLY; their individual articles were not read in this session, and that limitation is inherited and restated rather than quietly dropped. LIMB B IS THE OPPOSITE EVIDENTIAL CASE AND IS TREATED ACCORDINGLY. MIW HOLDS NO TEXT OF CLC 1992, OF THE FUND CONVENTION 1992 OR OF THE SUPPLEMENTARY FUND PROTOCOL 2003 - the corpus carries verified status facts and status placeholders only, and its family log expressly declines to assert the limits. NO CONVENTION TEXT IS QUOTED, NO ARTICLE NUMBER IS ASSERTED FOR ANY OF THE THREE INSTRUMENTS, AND ABOVE ALL NO MONETARY OR SPECIAL DRAWING RIGHT FIGURE IS ASSERTED ANYWHERE - not a tonnage-band limit, not a fund ceiling, not a contributing-oil threshold quantity. That follows the corpus's own explicit retrieval instruction, and it is the correct discipline in substance as well: the ceilings are amended by tacit acceptance over time, so a figure carried from any other source would be a currency risk as well as an evidential one. The tier ceilings are flagged in reverify_before_publication for verification against the official tables before publication. The three tiers are therefore described by their ARCHITECTURE - who is liable, who pays, and where the money comes from - which is precisely what the printed limb asks for and which is stable. All three instruments were in force well before this sitting; the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is the Indian statute giving effect to them, and the 2025 Act is three years future and is not cited.

questions.verification_status: Authored on the QP2406-Q9 route with all prose written fresh for this sitting, and with the donor audited backwards for sitting-relative content before any structure was reused. THIS QUESTION CARRIES NO STATUTORY CONTENT AND THE ANSWER SAYS SO EXPRESSLY: no IMO instrument, Indian statute or class rule prescribes a lubricating oil analysis programme, and none is named, so the answer does not borrow authority from an unrelated instrument. The techniques are carried at mechanism level as engineering and analytical-chemistry reference - atomic emission spectrometry by plasma or rotating-disc electrode arc with concentration read from emission intensity at characteristic wavelengths; the particle-size limitation arising from incomplete atomisation of coarse particles in the excitation source; infrared absorption at characteristic wavenumbers with Fourier transformation of the interferogram and differential comparison against the same oil unused; particle counting by optical light obscuration, by pore blockage on dark oil and by microscopy as referee, reported in cumulative size bands; and Base Number and Acid Number as separate titrations both expressed in milligrammes of potassium hydroxide per gramme. THE NO-FIGURES RULE IS ABSOLUTE AND IS THE MOST IMPORTANT EVIDENTIAL FEATURE OF THIS ANSWER: no condemning limit, alarm level, ppm value, cleanliness code, base number figure or wear rate appears anywhere as a general rule, because every one of them is engine-builder, oil, application and service specific and a figure carried between installations is a genuine hazard as well as an evidential defect. No standard number is asserted for either Base Number titration method. No oil company, analyser manufacturer, engine builder, laboratory or proprietary condition-monitoring programme is named. THE SINGLE DATED FACT IS THE 0.50 PER CENT M/M GLOBAL SULPHUR LIMIT, in force since 1 January 2020 and therefore three years and two months old at this sitting; it is used only to explain how cylinder oil base number is matched to the fuel actually burned, and no MARPOL Annex VI provision is quoted or numbered, consistent with the corpus holding that Annex as citation-ready and not quotation-ready under the 2026-08-11 freeze. The ISM Code is named at chapter 10 only as the regime under which sampling is planned and recorded; the held chain runs A.741(18) to MSC.353(92) and is the March 2023 text.

questions.question_text: Under Maritime law in case of a collision, explain following. (A) apportionment of damages (4) (B) proportionate fault (4) (C) collision liabilities (4) (D) presumptions of fault (4)
questions.short_title: Collision under Maritime Law - Apportionment, Proportionate Fault, Liabilities and Presumptions
regulations: Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules of Law with respect to Collisions between Vessels, Brussels 1910 (the Collision Convention) - the source of the doctrine; UNAMENDED. Proportionate liability by degree of fault; equal apportionment where the degrees cannot be established or the faults are equal; several liability for the vessels, cargoes and effects, and joint and several liability for loss of life and personal injury; the abolition of all legal presumptions of fault; and the two-year time bar

Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (India) - the statute giving effect to those rules at this sitting, and carrying the master's duty to stand by and render assistance after a collision, together with the presumption that follows a failure to do so. NO SECTION IS CITED BY NUMBER
COLREGs 1972 - the standard of conduct whose breach is the usual foundation of fault. Evidence of fault; NOT a presumption of causation

Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims (LLMC) - tonnage-based limitation, separate funds for claims for loss of life and personal injury and for property claims, and the conduct barring limitation. Identity level; NO FIGURE QUOTED
Civil Liability Convention 1992 and the Bunkers Convention 2001 - the strict, channelled pollution liability that runs alongside the fault-based collision claim. Named by identity and effect only
The collision liability (running down) clause in hull and machinery insurance - three-fourths of the liability to the other vessel. Commercial contract, not an instrument
The Both-to-Blame Collision Clause in bills of lading - the contractual answer to the cargo circularity created by several liability. Commercial contract, not an instrument
THE PENNSYLVANIA RULE - UNITED STATES LAW ONLY. Named as a contrast and expressly excluded as the applicable position

The material risk on this question is jurisdictional rather than temporal: the Pennsylvania Rule reverses the burden the Convention removed, and it is stated only as a contrast and expressly identified as United States law. No limitation figure and no apportionment percentage is offered as authority. The 7 July 2023 GHG boundary was assessed and does not engage this question.

questions.verification_status: This question is authored from first principles and from the settled architecture of the grain regime; MIW holds no donor and the corpus holds no copy of the International Grain Code. What is therefore stated with confidence, and what is stated with a recorded limitation, are deliberately separated. The MECHANISM - settlement and void formation, the slide of the grain surface to a new angle of repose, the transverse and vertical movement of G, the irreversibility of a dry-cargo shift as against a liquid free surface, and the consequent reduction in righting lever, maximum GZ, range and dynamical stability - is naval architecture and is derived rather than cited. The REGULATORY ARCHITECTURE - that bulk grain is governed by the International Grain Code adopted by resolution MSC.23(59) and made mandatory through SOLAS chapter VI, that a Document of Authorization is required, and that grain sits outside the IMSBC regime - is settled and is stated as such. The THREE NUMERICAL CRITERIA and the assumed heeling-arm construction are the part MIW cannot presently verify at source: they are universally published, they are the substance of what the question asks for, and they are given in full, but they are graded as authoritative secondary rather than primary and remain graded as authoritative secondary; SOLAS chapter VI regulations 8 and 9 were read at source in laptop review, which primary-verifies the Code identity, the statutory definition of grain, the mandatory hook and the Document of Authorization. No cargo property figure - stowage factor, bulk density or an actual angle of repose for any particular grain - is asserted anywhere, consistent with MIW's standing position on unverified cargo characteristics.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The three numerical grain stability criteria - 12 degrees or deck edge immersion whichever is lesser for ships constructed on or after 1 January 1994; residual area not less than 0.075 metre-radians measured to the least of the maximum-difference angle, 40 degrees and the flooding angle; and fluid initial GM not less than 0.30 m.
reverify_before_publication.why: MIW HOLDS NO COPY OF THE INTERNATIONAL GRAIN CODE. These are the substance of what the question asks for and are universally published, so they are given in full rather than withheld - but they are authoritative secondary knowledge, not text read at source. They should be checked against MSC.23(59) when a copy is acquired. This is the single largest evidence limitation on the paper and it is stated in the answer's own uncertainty section as well as here.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the assumed heeling arm is a straight line from its value at zero degrees to 0.8 of that value at forty degrees, the zero value being the total assumed volumetric heeling moment divided by stowage factor times displacement.
reverify_before_publication.why: Same limitation as the criteria - settled published construction, not read at source. It matters because the diagram is drawn from it and a candidate reproducing the answer draws a straight line on the strength of it.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the International Grain Code is adopted by resolution MSC.23(59) and made mandatory through SOLAS chapter VI, and that grain is outside the IMSBC Code.
reverify_before_publication.why: RESOLVED IN REVIEW. SOLAS chapter VI was read at source from the corpus copy of the Convention: regulation 8 defines the International Grain Code as the Code adopted by resolution MSC.23(59), and regulation 9 requires a cargo ship carrying grain to comply with it and to hold a Document of Authorization, the Code's requirements being "treated as mandatory". The reading is of the 2024 consolidated edition, which post-dates this sitting; regulation VI/9 is not among the provisions amended since, so the position at September 2023 is the same, and that edition point is the only residue. That grain sits outside the IMSBC Code remains authoritative secondary knowledge.

reverify_before_publication.why: A conventional working value from grain loading practice, given in the answer as such rather than as a Code figure. It is illustrative and no criterion depends on it.

questions.verification_status: The substance of this answer is deliberately re-anchored away from the donor's evidential base, and the reason is a wrong-edition risk that runs in the opposite direction to the usual one. The donor QP2404-Q8 rests on resolution A.1188(33), the 2023 Guidelines on implementation of the ISM Code by Administrations, which was adopted on 6 December 2023 and which revoked A.1118(30); its paragraph references are that resolution's numbering. At a September 2023 sitting A.1188(33) does not exist and the operative guidelines are A.1118(30) of 2017. MIW holds no copy of A.1118(30) and it has never been read at source, so its paragraph numbering is unknown and cannot be reconstructed. The answer is therefore built on material MIW does hold and which did not change: ISM Code section 13, certification and periodical verification, which is mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX and has been unamended since MSC.353(92) entered into force on 1 January 2015 - the corpus holds the full adopting and amending chain from A.741(18) to MSC.353(92) and its instrument log records MSC.353(92) as the latest amendment to the Code itself. To that is added MSC/Circ.1059-MEPC/Circ.401 of 16 December 2002 on procedures concerning observed ISM Code major non-conformities, which is operative at this sitting. A.1118(30) is cited BY IDENTITY ONLY, as the operative guidelines edition, and NOT ONE PARAGRAPH NUMBER FROM A.1188(33) IS CARRIED ACROSS. The QP2404 record's own read-at-source finding - that the substance of the paragraphs it used is largely unchanged between the two editions - is what makes the mandatory-text route safe; it is recorded as the reason and is not used as a licence to cite paragraphs nobody has read. The audit-and-survey distinction in limb (a) is definitional, is carried from the QP2404 record, and carries no temporal risk at all.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That resolution A.1118(30) of 2017 is the operative Guidelines on implementation of the ISM Code by Administrations at this sitting, A.1188(33) having been adopted on 6 December 2023 and having revoked it.
reverify_before_publication.why: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT FLAG ON THIS PAPER. Every other paper in the MIW corpus sits after 6 December 2023 and correctly cites the later resolution, and the QP2404 record expressly warns that citing A.1118(30) at ITS sitting would be a wrong-edition error. A reviewer moving between papers will therefore read this citation as stale and be tempted to 'correct' it forward, which would date the answer three months into the future. It must survive editing.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That no paragraph number from either edition of the implementation guidelines appears in this answer, and that the answer rests instead on ISM Code section 13 and the Code's own definitions.
reverify_before_publication.why: A deliberate construction, not an omission. MIW holds no copy of A.1118(30) and its paragraph numbering is unknown; the donor's paragraph references belong to the later edition. A future editor who adds paragraph references to 'improve' the answer would be citing text nobody has read.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the ISM Code text operative at this sitting is the text as amended by MSC.353(92), in force 1 January 2015, no later amendment to the Code itself being known.
reverify_before_publication.why: The corpus holds the full chain and its instrument log records MSC.353(92) as the latest amendment, with an open verification that no post-2013 amending resolution exists. That open item is recorded rather than relied on; a later amendment would in any event have to be in force before September 2023 to matter here.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the corpus ISM instrument log's identification of A.1184(33) as the ISM implementation guidelines conflicts with MIW's own read-at-source identification of A.1188(33) as that instrument, and that neither was consumed here.

Both resolutions post-date this sitting by three months, so the discrepancy could not affect this answer either way, and no new correction request is raised. questions.verification_status: The Convention's structure is carried at primary identity level and was confirmed against the MIW verification record for QP2301-Q5, where it was established for the January 2023 sitting: Article 1 on persons entitled to limit, Article 2 on claims subject to limitation, Article 3 on excepted claims, Article 4 on conduct barring limitation, Article 6 on the general limits and the two heads of claim, and Article 7 on the separate passenger limit. The critical distinction - that the TWO HEADS under Article 6 are loss of life or personal injury on the one hand and all other claims on the other, and that PASSENGER claims under Article 7 are a separate limit and NOT one of the two heads - is carried deliberately, because it is the point on which the limb turns. The dates were re-verified for this sitting: adoption 19 November 1976, entry into force 1 December 1986, the 1996 Protocol in force 13 May 2004, and the 2012 amendments effective 8 June 2015. NO MONETARY LIMIT, TONNAGE BAND OR SPECIAL DRAWING RIGHT FIGURE IS ASSERTED, because the Convention text was not read this session and the figures depend on which Protocol and which amendment a given State has adopted. THE INDIAN VEHICLE IS IDENTIFIED AS PART XA OF THE MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT, 1958 without asserting a ratification instrument or date that was not read this session. The four terms in limb b) are legal usage rather than treaty definitions, and the answer says so - only 'privity' has a specific historical anchor in the pre-1976 test, and that anchor is stated.

reverify_before_publication.why: A deliberate omission. The applicable figures depend on whether the State concerned is party to the bare 1976 Convention, the 1996 Protocol, or the Protocol as amended in 2012, and the Convention text was not read this session. The STRUCTURE of the limits is asserted; the numbers are not. Before publication, confirm no figure has been introduced by a later edit.

reverify_before_publication.why: The implementing vehicle is identified without asserting a ratification instrument, accession date or statutory sub-section that was not read this session. This is also the load-bearing jurisdictional statement for the sitting: the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 commenced 15 March 2026 and must not be carried into a 2023 answer.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the burden of proving the Article 4 conduct rests on the claimant
reverify_before_publication.why: Reflects the settled construction of the Convention and is the reason the right to limit is described as near-unbreakable. It rests on interpretation rather than on express words, and no judicial authority was read this session and none is cited.

reverify_before_publication.why: These are terms of general legal usage rather than definitions given in the Convention, and the answer states them as such. Only 'privity' has a specific anchor in maritime limitation law, in the pre-1976 'actual fault or privity' test, and that anchor is identified expressly.

The four load-bearing distinctions from CLC 92 - the WIDE shipowner definition with joint and several liability against CLC's EXCLUSIVE CHANNELLING to the registered owner; the ABSENCE of any free-standing limit, the Bunker Convention borrowing its ceiling from the applicable limitation regime; the ABSENCE of any fund behind it, against CLC's 1992 Fund and 2003 Supplementary Fund tiers; and the DIFFERENT INSURANCE THRESHOLD - are carried deliberately because they are what the closing limb turns on. The definitional boundary that 'bunker oil' is NOT confined to persistent oil and expressly includes lubricating oil and residues, where CLC is confined to persistent oil carried as cargo, is likewise carried deliberately. NO CONVENTION TEXT IS QUOTED VERBATIM; the definitions are given in substance at identity level. NO MONETARY LIMIT OR FUND CEILING IS ASSERTED, because those depend on the limitation regime and the amendments the State concerned has adopted and no Convention text was read this session. questions.verification_status: Verified against primary text, and the paper's principal temporal hazard is resolved inside this question rather than deferred to the anchor. RESOLUTION A.1185(33) WAS READ VERBATIM from the corpus copy: it is 'Procedures for port State control, 2023', ADOPTED 6 DECEMBER 2023, and its four operative clauses ADOPT the Procedures, INVITE Governments to implement them, REQUEST the Committees to keep them under review, and REVOKE resolution A.1155(32). ITS DOCUMENT COVER RECORDS THAT IT WAS ISSUED AS A DOCUMENT ON 2 JANUARY 2024 AND REISSUED ON 5 MARCH 2024 with editorial changes - so its text was not in circulation on any possible December 2023 examination day. Its recital identifies A.1155(32) as the Procedures for port State control, 2021, itself the successor to A.1138(31), A.1119(30), A.1052(27), A.882(21), A.787(19), A.742(18), A.597(15) and A.466(XII). NEITHER RESOLUTION CONTAINS ANY DEFERRED-EFFECT CLAUSE. Three consequences were adjudicated and are recorded in temporal_review: the instruments are RECOMMENDATORY, so the legal framework is created by the conventions and not by them; the inspection and detention structure the question asks about is unchanged across the boundary; and the 2023 text was not obtainable in December 2023. The answer therefore states the position without asserting which side of 6 December 2023 the sitting fell, and its correctness does not depend on the day. The right-of-appeal provision was read verbatim at paragraph 2.3.11 of the 2023 Procedures: the company or its representative have a right of appeal against a detention, the appeal should not cause the detention to be suspended, and the PSCO should properly inform the master. THE PARAGRAPH NUMBER IN THE 2021 EDITION IS NOT INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED, because A.1155(32) is not held in the corpus; the substance is stated as the content of section 2.3 of the Procedures and the paragraph reference is attributed to the 2023 text alone. THE CORPUS HOLDS NO MARINE-INSURANCE MATERIAL AT ALL - no York Antwerp Rules of any edition, no Marine Insurance Act 1963, no policy conditions. This question is therefore marked REFERENCE_PENDING against the corpus and is authored from established marine-insurance law and practice, which is declared in the answer rather than dressed up as a corpus citation. NO PROVISION HAS BEEN INVENTED AND NO RULE TEXT IS PRESENTED AS A VERBATIM QUOTATION FROM A SOURCE THAT WAS NOT READ. The definition of a general average act is given as the settled substance of Rule A - an extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure, intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety, for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure - and it is stated as the substance of the Rule rather than as a transcription. The conditions for declaring general average are given as the conditions the Rules and the case law impose, each identified separately so the examiner can count them. THE EXAMINER NAMED THE 1994 EDITION AND THAT CHOICE IS RESPECTED THROUGHOUT: the answer is written to the 1994 Rules, and the differences that matter between 1994 and 2016 - the commission and interest provisions, the absence of a time bar in the 1994 text, and the Rule Paramount - are stated as edition differences and not as amendments to law. The warranties limb is authored from the Indian Marine Insurance Act, 1963, whose provisions on warranties follow the English Act of 1906; the answer states which system each proposition comes from, and expressly records that the English reform of 2015 changed the English position on breach and is NOT the Indian rule. Section numbers are given for the Indian Act as established statutory content, and are flagged for verification against the Act itself in reverify_before_publication because the statute is not held in the corpus.

questions.verification_status: Verified to the extent the corpus permits, and the limit is stated rather than concealed. THE CORPUS HOLDS NO PSSA MATERIAL AND NO INDIAN ENVIRONMENTAL-LAW MATERIAL. Its India folder holds the Admiralty Act 2017, the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 and the Coastal Shipping Act 2025 - two of the three being FUTURE at this sitting and neither relevant here - and it does not hold the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, which is the operative statute. This question is therefore marked REFERENCE_PENDING against the corpus and is authored from the established content of the PSSA guidelines and of the Indian statutory framework, declared as such in the answer. NO PROVISION HAS BEEN INVENTED AND NO GUIDELINE TEXT IS PRESENTED AS A VERBATIM QUOTATION FROM A SOURCE THAT WAS NOT READ. THE ONE CLAIM MOST AT RISK OF DRIFT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT MADE. The number of PSSAs designated worldwide changes when the environment committee designates another, so no count appears in this object. What is stated is the load-bearing proposition - that designations are few, that the first was the Great Barrier Reef in 1990, and that NONE IS IN INDIAN WATERS - together with the related and equally load-bearing facts that no Indian sea area is a MARPOL Special Area and none is an Emission Control Area. Those are what make limb (a) a conditional question, and they are what the first mark is for. The distinction on which limb (b) turns - that a PSSA has NO legal effect of its own and that what regulates shipping is the Associated Protective Measure, so that a PSSA without an APM changes nothing a ship must do - is the settled architecture of the guidelines and is stated as such. THE SITTING-DAY QUESTION DOES NOT ARISE HERE: no Assembly resolution of December 2023 touches this question, and the PSSA guidelines are an environment committee instrument.

questions.verification_status: Verified to the extent the corpus permits, and the limit is stated rather than concealed. THE GOVERNING CIRCULAR IS NOT HELD IN THE CORPUS. The corpus GHG instrument log records the Revised FSA Guidelines circular explicitly as NOT HELD and carries it as an open placeholder. This question is therefore marked REFERENCE_PENDING against the corpus and is authored from the established content of those Guidelines, declared as such in the answer. NO PROVISION HAS BEEN INVENTED AND NO PASSAGE IS PRESENTED AS A VERBATIM QUOTATION FROM A SOURCE THAT WAS NOT READ. The five steps, the definitions of hazard and risk, the analytical techniques, the cost-effectiveness indices and the requirement that recommendations be presented in a form the decision maker can act on are stated in substance as the settled content of the method. WHAT THE CORPUS DOES SUPPORT, AND IT IS USED: the corpus's own note on this subject records the five-step structure and the essential distinction between FSA as an IMO RULE-MAKING TOOL and onboard risk assessment under the ISM Code, and that distinction is carried into the answer as the framing point. TWO PROPOSITIONS THAT ARE EASY TO GET WRONG WERE ADJUDICATED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. First, PROBLEM DEFINITION IS NOT ONE OF THE FIVE STEPS - it is the preparatory act by which the decision makers define the problem, the ship type or system and the scope, before step 1 begins; presenting it as step 1 and pushing hazard identification to step 2 is the commonest structural error on this question and the answer says so explicitly. Second, FSA DOES NOT SETTLE HOW MUCH RISK IS ACCEPTABLE. The method makes the criteria explicit and requires them to be stated; it does not supply a universally agreed acceptance threshold, and the answer states that limit rather than inventing a number. THE SITTING-DAY QUESTION DOES NOT ARISE HERE: the governing instrument is a committee circular, not an Assembly resolution, so the 6 December 2023 boundary does not touch this question.

NO IMO INSTRUMENT PRESCRIBES A HULL FORM AND NONE HAS BEEN INVENTED TO GIVE THIS ANSWER FALSE AUTHORITY. The hydrodynamics - the decomposition of resistance into frictional, wave-making and viscous pressure components; the propulsive coefficient and its hull efficiency term; wake fraction and thrust deduction; the mechanism by which a bulbous bow cancels part of the bow wave system and why that cancellation is tuned to a particular speed and draught; the relationship between wake uniformity, cavitation, pressure pulses and vibration; and the wetted-surface against propulsive-efficiency trade that decides whether a twin skeg arrangement pays - is standard naval architecture and is explained mechanistically rather than asserted. The only regulatory claims are the framing statements at step 6, and those were read from the corpus copy of the 2021 revised MARPOL Annex VI (MEPC.328(76)): chapter 4 and regulations 22 and 24 for EEDI, regulations 23 and 25 for EEXI and regulation 28 for the operational carbon intensity indicator, with both EEXI and CII correctly stated as in force since 1 January 2023 at this sitting. NO NUMERIC PERCENTAGE SAVING IS QUOTED ANYWHERE for a bow retrofit, an aftbody reshaping or a twin skeg arrangement - all are design-specific, and section 2.1 requires an unverifiable quantity to be omitted rather than given false precision. THE PRINTED PHRASE 'TWIN SKEG DESIGN' IS AMBIGUOUS and the answer states which reading it takes - the twin-screw twin-skeg arrangement - rather than resolving it silently. Energy saving devices are expressly distinguished from hull form rather than blurred into aftbody optimisation. Nothing from MEPC 81, which sat five weeks after this examination, appears anywhere. LAPTOP CORRECTION (Batch 1 integration review): the MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 regulation numbering in this object was wrong and has been corrected against the corpus copy of MEPC.328(76) read directly. Regulation 21 is Functional requirements, NOT EEDI; attained EEDI is regulation 22 and required EEDI regulation 24. Regulation 25 is Required EEXI; attained EEXI is regulation 23. The desktop referral named QP2402-Q3 only; the same mis-numbering was present in Q5 and the EEXI half of it in Q6, and all three were corrected together. Regulation 25.3 (review by 1 January 2026) was checked against the resolution and is correct as it stood.

This is instrumental analysis and machinery condition monitoring: NO IMO OR STATUTORY INSTRUMENT PRESCRIBES A LUBRICATING OIL ANALYSIS PROGRAMME, and none is named, so the answer does not borrow authority from an unrelated instrument. The techniques are described at mechanism level and carried as engineering and analytical-chemistry reference: atomic emission spectrometry by plasma or rotating-disc electrode; the particle-size limitation arising from incomplete atomisation of large particles in the excitation source; infrared absorption at characteristic wavenumbers with Fourier transformation of the interferogram and differential comparison against the unused oil; particle counting by optical light obscuration, pore blockage or microscopy, reported in cumulative size bands; and Base Number and Acid Number as separate titrations expressed in milligrammes of potassium hydroxide per gramme. THE NO-FIGURES RULE IS ABSOLUTE AND IS THE MOST IMPORTANT EVIDENTIAL FEATURE OF THIS ANSWER: no condemning limit, alarm level, ppm value, ISO cleanliness code, base number figure or wear rate is quoted as a general rule anywhere, because every one is engine-builder, oil, application and service specific, and a figure carried between installations is a genuine hazard as well as an evidential defect. No standard number is asserted for either Base Number titration method; the two methods are distinguished by their chemistry and by the direction of the discrepancy between them. No oil company, analyser manufacturer, engine builder, laboratory or proprietary condition-monitoring programme is named. The single dated fact is the 0.50 per cent m/m global sulphur limit for fuel outside emission control areas, in force since 1 January 2020, four and a half years before this sitting, used only to explain cylinder oil base number selection; no MARPOL Annex VI provision is quoted or numbered, consistent with the corpus holding that Annex as citation-ready only.

questions.verification_status: This is a pure marine-engineering question with no statutory content and no primary instrument to read, and the evidence position is stated plainly rather than dressed up. The engine described is the electronically controlled two-stroke crosshead engine as it is universally built and operated, and the answer is written from first principles and from standard shipboard practice: what a camshaft did, what replaced it, how a hydraulic intensifier develops injection pressure, and what electronic control of the timing buys and costs. NO ENGINE BUILDER, MODEL DESIGNATION OR PROPRIETARY SYSTEM NAME IS USED EXCEPT WHERE THE STEM ITSELF USES IT - the stem names ME, MC, HPS, HCU, ELFI and FIVA, and those terms are therefore used and explained; nothing further is named. NO QUANTITY IS ASSERTED ANYWHERE ON THIS QUESTION. No hydraulic system pressure, no injection pressure, no filtration rating, no specific fuel oil consumption figure, no percentage improvement at part load and no minimum stable load figure appears. Each of those is a builder-specific and variant-specific number, MIW holds no licensed copy of any engine builder's project guidance or operating manual, and PASTPAPER_PRODUCTION_PROTOCOL.md section 2.1 requires an unverifiable quantity to be omitted rather than given false precision. The mechanisms are described qualitatively and completely, which is what the stem asks for and what earns the marks. Where engine variants genuinely differ - most importantly, whether the exhaust valve retains mechanical actuation - the answer says that variants differ rather than presenting one arrangement as universal.

questions.verification_status: Written entirely from resolution MEPC.377(80), the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, read at source this session in full - the operative paragraphs, the levels of ambition, the indicative checkpoints, the guiding principles, the candidate measures by timeline, the impact-assessment criteria, the follow-up table and the review clause. THIS IS THE PAPER'S HIGHEST TEMPORAL RISK AND THE ANCHOR NAMES IT AS ONE OF TWO DECISIVE EXCLUSIONS. At July 2024 the answer to 'the IMO's revised strategy' is MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023 - almost exactly one year before the sitting - and NOTHING LATER. Everything the industry now associates with the mid-term measures belongs to 2025: the approved basket, the IMO Net-Zero Framework, the Global Fuel Intensity mechanism and the pricing element. None of it appears here, and the answer states the position the Strategy itself set out - the basket to be finalized and agreed by 2025, approved at MEPC 83 in spring 2025 and adopted at an extraordinary session thereafter, with entry into force sixteen months after adoption. MEPC 81 (March 2024) had taken place four months before the sitting and MEPC 82 (September-October 2024) had not; the answer says only what follows from the Strategy's own timetable and asserts no MEPC 81 or MEPC 82 outcome. Every numeric target quoted - 40%, 5% striving for 10%, 20% striving for 30% by 2030, 70% striving for 80% by 2040, net zero by or around 2050 - is quoted from the resolution text, as are the 2.2% and 2.89% emission-share figures, which appear in the Strategy's own introduction. No unverifiable quantity is asserted anywhere.

questions.verification_status: THIS IS A PURE NAVAL ARCHITECTURE AND MARINE ENGINEERING QUESTION WITH NO STATUTORY CONTENT, AND THE EVIDENCE POSITION IS STATED PLAINLY RATHER THAN DRESSED UP. MIW holds no naval-architecture text, no model-test data, no towing-tank or CFD results and no builder's project guidance. The resistance decomposition, the effect of length, beam, draught and fullness on each component, the economy of scale in displacement against wetted surface, the consequences for installed power and engine selection, and the counter-pressures from stability, subdivision, strength, seakeeping and tonnage measurement are all STANDARD, NON-PROPRIETARY ENGINEERING reasoned from first principles and from standard practice, and are declared as such. NO QUANTITY IS ASSERTED ANYWHERE ON THIS QUESTION - no block or prismatic coefficient value, no length-to-beam or beam-to-draught ratio, no Froude number, no admiralty coefficient, no percentage fuel or power saving, no speed in knots, no deadweight figure and no EEDI value, phase, reduction factor or reference-line constant. THE ONLY QUANTITATIVE RELATIONSHIP USED IS THE APPROXIMATELY CUBIC POWER-SPEED RELATIONSHIP, AND IT IS PRESENTED AS AN APPROXIMATION AND AN IDEALISATION with its limitations stated - the exponent varies with hull form, loading condition and Froude number, rises sharply once significant wave-making begins, and is unreliable at very low load - and it is NOT used to compute a numerical saving. The MIW house treatment of hull-form parameters as qualitative, established across QP2410, QP2409, QP2404, QP2506 and QP2411, was confirmed this session and is followed without exception. QP2502-Q8 was read specifically to fix the boundary between hull-form optimisation, which is this question, and appendage retrofitting, which is not, so that the two MIW answers do not overlap or contradict. AN EARLIER SITTING OF THIS STEM EXISTS OUTSIDE THE MIW SOURCE SET AND HAS NOT BEEN TRANSCRIBED, so the earlier member cannot be read and is NOT treated as a donor.

questions.verification_status: THIS IS A PURE MARINE ENGINEERING QUESTION WITH NO STATUTORY CONTENT AND NO PRIMARY INSTRUMENT TO READ, AND THE EVIDENCE POSITION IS STATED PLAINLY. The energy balance of a large marine diesel engine, the existence of a surplus of exhaust energy at high load once the compressor's demand is met, the mechanism by which a power turbine, a hybrid machine and an electrically assisted turbocharger each act on that balance, the low-load and transient air deficit, and the maintenance, control and electrical-plant consequences of each arrangement are all STANDARD, NON-PROPRIETARY ENGINEERING reasoned from first principles and from standard shipboard and shipbuilding practice, and are declared as such. NO ENGINE BUILDER, TURBOCHARGER MAKER, MODEL DESIGNATION OR PROPRIETARY SYSTEM NAME IS USED ANYWHERE - the stem names none and MIW holds no builder's project guidance, no maker's manual and no product literature. NO QUANTITY IS ASSERTED ANYWHERE: no percentage of fuel energy in the exhaust, no percentage of power recovered, no electrical output, no efficiency figure, no specific fuel consumption improvement, no minimum engagement load, no turbocharger speed, no pressure ratio and no temperature. WHERE ENGINE AND INSTALLATION VARIANTS GENUINELY DIFFER THE ANSWER SAYS SO RATHER THAN PRESENTING ONE ARRANGEMENT AS UNIVERSAL - notably whether a power turbine drives a dedicated generator, is geared into the shaft line or is combined with a steam turbine on an exhaust gas boiler, and whether a hybrid's electrical machine is integrated in the turbocharger casing or mounted externally. The overlap between industry usage of 'hybrid' and 'electro-assist' is DECLARED rather than concealed: the answer distinguishes them by direction of energy flow, which is what makes the stem's three-way split intelligible, and states expressly that the categories are not watertight. The word 'latest' in the printed stem is NOT converted into a claim of novelty about any device, which would be unverifiable from held sources and a currency exposure at any sitting. No classification society rule is cited.

questions.question_text: How can Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR) technologies be integrated into training, operations and maintenance practices within the maritime industry to enhance safety, efficiency and decision-making? What are the potential challenges and benefits of implementing these technologies on board vessels or at maritime facilities? (16)
questions.short_title: Virtual and Augmented Reality in Maritime Training and Maintenance
regulations: STCW Convention and Code - the simulator regime permitting training and assessment by simulator and setting standards for simulators and for those conducting and assessing simulator-based training. Cited at regime level only; no provision is quoted and MIW holds no text-bearing copy
questions.family_summary: Set once in the sittings MIW has transcribed.
questions.verification_status: FRESH RESEARCH, NO DONOR. This question sets no instrument and the answer does not invent one. NO IMO OR STATUTORY INSTRUMENT PRESCRIBES THE USE OF VR OR AR, AND NONE HAS BEEN NAMED TO GIVE THE ANSWER FALSE AUTHORITY. The one regulatory anchor that is genuinely available is the STCW simulator regime - the Convention permits training and assessment by simulator and sets standards for simulator performance and for the conduct of simulator-based training - and it is used only to make the single point that an immersive trainer is not automatically a recognised means of demonstrating competence. That statement is made at the level of the regime, not by quoting provisions, because MIW holds no licensed STCW Code text and the 2017 consolidated edition in the corpus carries no text layer. The technical content - stereoscopic head-mounted display, six-degree-of-freedom tracking, motion-to-photon latency and simulator sickness, registration and tracking error in AR, the difference between a rendered environment and an overlay on the real one - is engineering and human-factors reference class and is declared as such under PASTPAPER_PRODUCTION_PROTOCOL section 2.1. NO ADOPTION FIGURE, COST, TRAINING-TIME SAVING OR RETENTION PERCENTAGE IS QUOTED ANYWHERE. Vendor products, headset models and class-society branded services are named nowhere. NOTHING POST-DATING NOVEMBER 2024 APPEARS.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That simulator-based training and assessment must satisfy the STCW simulator standards, and that an immersive trainer is therefore not automatically a recognised means of demonstrating competence.
reverify_before_publication.why: This is the only regulatory proposition in the answer and it is stated at REGIME level, not from the instrument text, because MIW holds no STCW Code copy with a usable text layer - the 2017 consolidated edition in the corpus is image-only. Acquiring a text-bearing STCW Code would promote this to primary and allow the relevant regulation and Code section to be cited. Recorded as an accepted limitation rather than a blocker because the proposition is not controversial and the answer claims no more than the regime plainly provides.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The verdict at step 6 that maintenance guidance, familiarisation and remote support are commercially established while assessment for certification and safety-critical operational use are not.
reverify_before_publication.why: This is engineering and commercial judgement reasoned from the properties of the two technologies, not a surveyed finding, and it is declared as such. It is also the most date-sensitive statement in the answer. THIS ANSWER IS ANCHORED TO NOVEMBER 2024 AND MUST NOT BE UPDATED IN PLACE - a later reader who refreshes it to the current state of the market destroys exactly what makes it correct for this paper.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That no IMO or statutory instrument governs the use of VR or AR at this sitting.
reverify_before_publication.why: An assertion of ABSENCE, which is the hardest class to verify. It was established by searching the corpus instrument holdings and finding no instrument on the subject, and by the fact that the industry treats immersive training as supplementary to approved training rather than as an approved route. If an instrument on immersive training is ever found to pre-date November 2024, this answer changes. Note the direction of the risk: the danger is a later development being read back into this sitting.

reverify_before_publication.claim: No adoption, cost, training-time, retention or accident-reduction figure is quoted anywhere, and no product, vendor or classification society is named.

ONE INSTRUMENT WAS READ AT SOURCE: resolution MSC.255(84), adopted 16 May 2008, adopting the Code of the International Standards and Recommended Practices for a Safety Investigation into a Marine Casualty or Marine Incident - the Casualty Investigation Code - from the MIW True Source corpus. Its identity and adoption date were read off the resolution, and it is used for the proposition that the international standard for casualty investigation is directed at identifying circumstances and causes so that safety may be enhanced, which is the regulatory expression of looking beyond the last unsafe act. THE REMAINING INSTRUMENT REFERENCES ARE AUTHORITATIVE RESTATEMENT AND ARE CLASSIFIED P2. In particular, IMO resolution A.947(23), the Human Element Vision, Principles and Goals for the Organization, IS NOT HELD BY MIW; it is cited by identity only for the Organization's own framing of the human element as a complex multi-dimensional issue spanning the whole industry, and NO TEXT IS QUOTED AND NO PARAGRAPH IS ASSERTED. questions.verification_status: FRESH RESEARCH, NO DONOR. THIS IS AN INSTRUMENTAL-ANALYSIS AND MACHINERY-CONDITION QUESTION AND IT CARRIES NO REGULATORY CONTENT. NO IMO INSTRUMENT PRESCRIBES A LUBRICATING OIL ANALYSIS PROGRAMME AND NONE HAS BEEN NAMED TO GIVE THIS ANSWER FALSE AUTHORITY. The physics and chemistry - atomic emission from an excited plasma or arc and the particle-size dependence that follows from incomplete atomisation of large particles; infrared absorption at characteristic wavenumbers by specific molecular bonds and the differential measurement against a new-oil reference spectrum; optical light-obscuration and pore-blockage particle counting and the interference from water droplets, air and soot; and acid-base titration of an alkaline additive reserve against accumulated strong and weak acids - is declared as ENGINEERING AND ANALYTICAL-CHEMISTRY REFERENCE under PASTPAPER_PRODUCTION_PROTOCOL section 2.1 and is explained mechanistically rather than asserted. TEST-METHOD AND REPORTING STANDARDS ARE NAMED BY IDENTITY ONLY AND ARE NOT HELD BY MIW: the ISO cleanliness code for particle-count reporting, and the two distinct standard titration methods for Base Number which give systematically different results on the same oil. THAT LAST POINT IS RECORDED AS A REAL PRACTICAL TRAP AND IS DECLARED AS RESTATEMENT, NOT AS PRIMARY. NO CONDEMNING LIMIT, ALARM LEVEL, PPM VALUE, CLEANLINESS CODE OR BN FIGURE IS QUOTED AS A GENERAL RULE ANYWHERE: every such value is engine-builder, oil-company and application specific, and section 2.1 requires an unverifiable quantity to be omitted rather than given false precision. The characteristic infrared wavenumbers are given as approximate positions because they are properties of the molecular bonds themselves rather than of any instrument or standard, and are declared as such.
