questions.family_summary: Set once in the sittings MIW has transcribed.
questions.verification_status: Verified against primary sources at the December 2024 sitting date. The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly by resolution A/RES/70/1 on 25 September 2015 and came into effect on 1 January 2016, comprising 17 Sustainable Development Goals and 169 targets, organised around the five areas of People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace and Partnership, with the central pledge to leave no one behind; progress is reviewed through the High-Level Political Forum and voluntary national reviews, and measured against a global indicator framework. The maritime limb was anchored instrument by instrument at the sitting date. The operative IMO climate instrument is the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, resolution MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 July 2023, which superseded the 2018 Initial Strategy: net-zero GHG emissions from international shipping by or around, i.e. close to, 2050; indicative checkpoints for 2030 and 2040; and uptake of zero or near-zero GHG emission technologies, fuels and energy sources by 2030. The short-term measures - EEXI, the operational CII and the enhanced SEEMP - entered into force 1 January 2023, so 2023 is the first full CII data year and the first ratings were issued during 2024. MEPC 82, held 30 September to 4 October 2024, continued work on the mid-term measures and opened the review of the short-term measures, referring it to a correspondence group and an intersessional working group reporting to MEPC 83 in 2025; NO mid-term measure had been adopted at this sitting and none is described as adopted. For SDG 14 the instruments relied on are MARPOL Annexes I to VI, the Ballast Water Management Convention 2004 (in force 8 September 2017), the AFS Convention 2001, and the London Convention and Protocol. The Hong Kong International Convention for the Safe and Environmentally Sound Recycling of Ships, 2009 was verified separately: its entry-into-force criteria were met in June 2023 when Bangladesh and Liberia became Contracting States, and it enters into force 24 months later on 26 JUNE 2025 - which is SIX MONTHS AFTER this examination, so at this sitting it is adopted and ratified but NOT YET IN FORCE, and the answer says so expressly.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, resolution MEPC.377(80) of 7 July 2023, is the operative strategy at this sitting, having superseded the 2018 Initial Strategy
reverify_before_publication.why: Anchored to the sitting date. Do not revert to the 2018 Initial Strategy, and do not advance to any later strategy or measure. The 2023 Strategy is correct for December 2024.

reverify_before_publication.claim: No IMO mid-term GHG measure had been adopted at this sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: DO NOT ADD ONE. The mid-term measures were under development and the work was referred onward to MEPC 83 in 2025, after this examination. An editor working from current material would find measures adopted and would introduce a state of affairs that did not exist at the sitting.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The Hong Kong International Convention 2009 was adopted and ratified but NOT YET IN FORCE at this sitting, entering into force 26 June 2025
reverify_before_publication.why: DO NOT UPDATE THIS. The Convention entered into force six months AFTER this examination. Current material describes it as in force; changing it here would destroy the adopted-versus-in-force point the answer is built on and would be wrong for a December 2024 sitting.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That no figure is asserted for shipping's share of global greenhouse gas emissions or of world trade
reverify_before_publication.why: Both figures circulate very widely and are quoted at materially different values by different sources and study years. None was verified for this sitting and the argument is deliberately made qualitatively. If a figure is added later it must be sourced and dated at or before December 2024.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The numerical values of the 2030 and 2040 indicative checkpoints in the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy are described in structure rather than quoted
reverify_before_publication.why: The checkpoint values were not re-read from the resolution text in this session. The structure - a percentage reduction in total annual GHG emissions against a 2008 baseline, stated as a minimum with a higher striving-for level - IS established, as are the net-zero-by-or-around-2050 and 2030 zero or near-zero fuel ambitions. If the figures are added later they must come from MEPC.377(80) itself.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That no SDG progress statistic or count of voluntary national reviews is asserted
reverify_before_publication.why: UN progress reporting is published annually and none was verified for December 2024.

questions.verification_status: Verified against the Paris MoU's published procedures and against authoritative industry guidance, anchored to the December 2024 sitting. The New Inspection Regime entered into force on 1 January 2011, replacing the previous target factor with a ship risk profile and replacing the 25 per cent individual inspection commitment with a shared commitment to inspect all ships visiting the region. The Ship Risk Profile parameters, the three risk categories, the periodic inspection windows (High Risk 5 to 6 months, Standard Risk 10 to 12 months, Low Risk 24 to 36 months), the Priority I and Priority II definitions, the overriding and unexpected factor triggers, the inspection types and the expanded-inspection population (every High Risk Ship, and every bulk carrier, chemical tanker, gas carrier, oil tanker or passenger ship older than 12 years), the ETA72, ETA24, ATA and ATD reporting obligations, the THETIS database fed through SafeSeaNet, and the refusal-of-access criteria and durations (black-listed flag banned after the third detention in 36 months; grey-listed flag after the third detention in 24 months; any detention after the second ban; lifting after 3 months, 12 months, 24 months, then permanent) were all established from those sources. Sitting-date position verified separately: the performance lists operative at this examination are the 2023 lists, approved at the 57th Committee meeting and applied from 1 July 2024; the Russian Federation is suspended from the Paris MoU; and the Ship Risk Profile revisions aligned with the recast EU Port State Control Directive were still in preparation, that Directive applying from 2027, so they are recorded as future and not as operative.

Current Paris MoU material will describe them as adopted or in force; introducing them would be future contamination in a December 2024 paper.

reverify_before_publication.why: Anchored to the sitting date. Guidance issued at the NIR's introduction lists the Russian Federation as a full member and describes its national system as feeding THETIS; that description is stale and must not be reinstated.

questions.verification_status: Verified against the conventions and the Indian implementing statutes as at the December 2024 sitting. The Hague Rules 1924 and the Hague-Visby Rules (the 1968 Visby Protocol and the 1979 SDR Protocol) were used for the definition of 'carriage of goods' as covering the period from the time when the goods are loaded on to the time they are discharged from the ship (Article I(e)); the carrier's obligations of due diligence to make the ship seaworthy before and at the beginning of the voyage and properly and carefully to load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods (Article III rules 1 and 2); the catalogue of exceptions (Article IV rule 2(a) to (q)) including the nautical fault and fire exceptions, perils of the sea, inherent defect quality or vice of the goods, insufficiency of packing, latent defects not discoverable by due diligence, and the catch-all at (q) with its burden of proof on the carrier; the package or unit limitation as amended by the Visby and SDR Protocols; and the one-year time bar under Article III rule 6. The Hamburg Rules 1978 were used for the port-to-port period of responsibility (Article 4) and the presumed-fault basis of liability (Article 5). The Rotterdam Rules 2008 were used for the door-to-door period (Articles 11 and 12) and are recorded as ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE at this sitting. The Indian position at this sitting was established as: the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925, amended in 1993 to give effect to the Hague-Visby Rules, together with the Indian Bills of Lading Act 1856; India is not a party to the Hamburg Rules or the Rotterdam Rules. No post-2024 Indian carriage legislation appears anywhere in this object.

A later editor working from current Indian law would substitute the replacement statutes and would introduce law that did not exist at this sitting. Gas carriers of 15,000 DWT and above, all containerships, general cargo ships, LNG carriers and cruise passenger ships ran Phase 2 from 1 January 2020 to 31 MARCH 2022 and entered Phase 3 on 1 APRIL 2022; bulk carriers, the smaller gas-carrier bands, tankers, refrigerated cargo carriers, combination carriers and all ro-ro classes ran Phase 2 from 1 January 2020 to 31 DECEMBER 2024 and entered Phase 3 on 1 JANUARY 2025. AT THIS MARCH 2025 SITTING PHASE 2 IS THEREFORE CLOSED ON BOTH TIMETABLES, the second having closed only TEN WEEKS BEFORE THE PAPER. The printed stem's premise - 'the PRESENT EEDI framework under Phase 2' - is accordingly false at this sitting, and it is PRESERVED AND ADJUDICATED rather than corrected away, because the design content the stem asks for is phase-independent and is delivered in full. The corpus record itself names the transplantation of one timetable onto the other as 'the unit's most transplantable error', and warns that applying one to the other's ships shifts a 30 per cent obligation by two years and nine months. The corpus's export policy is facts-and-pointers-only, so identity, structure, duty-bearers and numerics are used and NO BODY TEXT IS REPRODUCED. The regulation identities and the verification architecture are carried from QP2502-Q6, the immediately preceding sitting, whose temporal record establishes that regulation 22 is unamended, that MEPC.385(81) - deemed accepted 1 February 2025 - operates on regulations 2, 13, 14, 18 and 27 and touches no EEDI regulation, and that MEPC.392(82) is adopted only with entry into force 1 March 2026. The physical content is therefore ESTABLISHED NAVAL ARCHITECTURE AND MARINE ENGINEERING and is stated as such: the decomposition of resistance, the mechanism by which roughness thickens the boundary layer and raises frictional resistance, the behaviour of antifouling coating systems, the propulsive efficiency chain and the effect of blade surface condition on torque and thrust are engineering fact and depend on no instrument. The IMO Biofouling Guidelines are cited BY IDENTITY AND EFFECT ONLY - they are GUIDANCE, not law, they are not held by the corpus and were not read, and NO resolution number, edition or paragraph is asserted. The AFS Convention is named only for the boundary it draws on coating chemistry, and its cybutryne control - whose 1 January 2023 entry into force predates this sitting by more than two years - is stated as operative without asserting any AFS provision number, since the corpus does not hold that Convention either. The corpus holds NO P&I material. true-source/08-industry-organisations/INDUSTRY_SOURCES.md is expressly labelled 'Storage class: citation/index only - official web sources listed; no PDFs held', and its P&I entry records the concept at outline level only: that P&I means Protection (crew injury and death, collision liabilities to third parties, wreck removal, pollution beyond hull policies) and Indemnity (cargo claims, fines); that clubs are mutual and member-owned and raise CALLS rather than premiums; that twelve clubs pool large claims through the International Group pooling agreement and collective reinsurance; and that the club differs from ordinary fixed-premium, profit-making insurance by mutuality, breadth of cover and the absence of a fixed sum insured. igpandi.org is named as the source. NO CLUB RULE BOOK, NO POOLING AGREEMENT AND NO INTERNATIONAL GROUP DOCUMENT IS HELD. Every statement about club rules, cover, calls and claims procedure is therefore carried at INDUSTRY GUIDANCE level; NO RULE NUMBER, NO MONETARY LIMIT, NO POOLING RETENTION FIGURE AND NO REINSURANCE ATTACHMENT POINT IS QUOTED anywhere in the answer, because none can be sourced. THE STATUTORY FRAME IS PRIMARY. The Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 is held as an official India Code text and was read directly: section 4(1) lists as maritime claims the very heads a club insures against - (e) loss of life or personal injury, (f) loss or damage to goods, (o) crew wages and repatriation, (u) environmental damage and the cost of preventive and restoration measures, (v) wreck raising and removal, and (s) insurance premium including MUTUAL INSURANCE CALLS, which is the statute's own recognition of the club call. Section 5 gives the arrest power that makes club security commercially necessary, and section 11 the protection against wrongful arrest. The Marine Insurance Act, 1963 is named as the governing Indian statute at this sitting and, per the corpus's own note, its subrogation section is recorded as REQUIRING VERIFICATION, so no section number is cited for it. INTERNAL REUSE: QP2502-Q7 (February 2025), built - supplied limbs (a) and (b), which are word-for-word identical, re-delivered at 5 marks each instead of 8; limb (c) is fresh.

questions.verification_status: AUTHORED FRESH. This is the only question on the paper with no donor and no family member, and it is also the least corpus-supported: the True Source corpus holds NO charter-party form, NO BIMCO document, NO P&I club rulebook and NO policy wording, and it holds CLC and the Bunkers Convention at citation and index level only. The answer is therefore built on settled structure and is explicit about its evidence class throughout. The discipline applied is the same one used on the paper's other gapped questions - refuse precision rather than invent it. Accordingly: no form edition, revision year or clause number is asserted; no package or unit limitation figure is quoted; no apportionment percentage from any inter-club cargo-claims agreement is asserted; no section number of the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 is asserted; and NO CASE AUTHORITY IS CITED ANYWHERE. The two load-bearing legal points are stated by Article and by effect rather than by quotation: CLC 1992 Article III(4) CHANNELS liability to the registered owner and bars claims against a charterer howsoever described, including a bareboat charterer, save for that person's own act or omission committed with intent or recklessly and with knowledge that such damage would probably result; and the 2001 Bunkers Convention Article 1(3) defines 'shipowner' WIDELY to include the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator, so that a BAREBOAT charterer is within the liable class where a time or voyage charterer is not. That contrast is the answer to limb (d) and it is the same distinction the MIW known-traps register records. The HNS Convention 2010 was not in force at this sitting and is stated as not in force rather than listed as available.

questions.short_title: Main Engine Failure to Respond to Bridge Control
questions.family_summary: Returns in the same words from March 2024 Q8.
questions.verification_status: Verified as an operational and procedural answer, and honestly bounded. The fault tree, the temporary measures and the permanent measures are Chief Engineer engineering judgement grounded in the architecture of a bridge-control installation - control transmitter, remote control system, safety and interlock logic, control air, starting air, reversing arrangement and fuel. Nothing unsafe is recommended: the answer expressly forbids resetting or overriding protective trips before the cause is established. The ISM Code elements and the SOLAS chapter II-1 bridge-control requirements are referred to at the level of their well-known effect and are FLAGGED as not read in a licensed consolidated edition this session, consistent with the posture already taken on the ISM Code in Q5 of this paper. No clause is quoted.

reverify_before_publication.why: The ISM Code was not read in a licensed consolidated edition this session. reverify_before_publication.why: ENGINEERING_JUDGEMENT throughout. No instrument prescribes them. A senior marine engineer review before publication would be appropriate; a regulatory check would find nothing to check.

reverify_before_publication.why: Deliberate. The stem specifies neither engine type nor control architecture, so a fault tree is the correct treatment and the answer says so. Recorded so that a later editor does not "improve" it by choosing one cause.

Verified from it: the light running margin defined as LRM = (nL - nH) / nH x 100 per cent, with MAN's own recommendation of 4 to 7 per cent depending on the specific ship and operational profile and up to 10 per cent in special cases; the rule of thumb that a 20 per cent increase in required power from added resistance corresponds to about 1 per cent heavy running, that is 1 per cent lower rpm for the same engine power; the engine load diagram limit lines, in particular that LINE 4 IS THE TORQUE/SPEED LIMIT, LIMITED MAINLY BY THE THERMAL LOAD ON THE ENGINE, that line 5 is the maximum mean effective pressure for continuous operation and is a limit only at high loads and speeds while at lower speeds line 4 is the stricter limit, that line 6 is the light propeller curve for clean hull and calm weather, and that line 8 is the overload limit permitting overload running only for limited periods, one hour per twelve hours or when required in an emergency; that class rules generally do not allow an engine to run faster than 115 per cent of SMCR rpm; that frictional resistance increases with fouling of the hull by algae, sea grass and barnacles; that shallow water in general has no influence when the water depth is more than ten times the ship's draught; and that in the bollard pull condition a heavy running factor of 15 to 20 per cent relative to the light propeller curve has been experienced, equivalent to approximately a 60 to 100 per cent increase in power for the same rpm. Sea margin is recorded as typically 10 to 30 per cent with 15 per cent historically applied, and engine margin typically 10 to 30 per cent with 10 per cent historically applied, both from the same document.

questions.verification_status: Verified against primary sources, and the highest-risk claim on the paper was tested and rejected. THE QUESTION'S FRAMING INVITES A FALSE STATEMENT, AND THE ANSWER DOES NOT MAKE IT. The IMO's own record of designated Particularly Sensitive Sea Areas was checked: nineteen PSSAs have been designated and NONE of them is in India. Neither the Lakshadweep islands nor the Andaman and Nicobar Islands holds PSSA designation. The question asks how these islands COULD be protected, and it is answered prospectively and accurately as such. The governing PSSA instrument was confirmed as resolution A.982(24) as amended by resolution MEPC.267(68). The Indian statutory position was established at a sitting date falling after the commencement of the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 on 15 March 2026.

The precise citation is not asserted and should be settled from the Gazette before publication.
